evidence.label: Public page: Evidence on concise, concrete web messaging and how unclear or generic copy affects comprehension
evidence.text: Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective: How to Write for the Web - NN/G Skip to content Nielsen Norman Group Nielsen Norman Group UX Training & Courses Live Online All Live Online Courses Upcoming Live Online Training Train Your Team Group-Discount Pricing Private Team Training UX Certification Self-Paced Self-Paced Courses New Deciding Between Formats? Find the training option that fits your learning style. Which Format Is Right For Me? Articles & Resources Articles & Videos Reports & Books The NN/G UX Podcast Consulting All Consulting Services Customized Research Expert Review Intensive Applied Workshops Keynote Speaking User Testing UX Maturity Assessment About Us About NNGroup People Clients News & Careers FAQs Contact Us Search Profile 26 Concise, SCANNABLE, and Objective: How to Write for the Web John Morkes, Jakob Nielsen John Morkes and Jakob Nielsen January 1, 1997 1997-01-01 Share Email article Share on LinkedIn Share on Twitter Summary: Studies of how users read on the Web found that they do not actually read: instead, they scan the text. A study of five different writing styles found that a sample Web site scored 58% higher in measured usability when it was written concisely, 47% higher when the text was scannable, and 27% higher when it was written in an objective style instead of the promotional style used in the control condition and many current Web pages. Combining these three changes into a single site that was concise, scannable, and objective at the same time resulted in 124% higher measured usability. Unfortunately, this paper is written in a print writing style and is somewhat too academic in style. We know this is bad, but the paper was written as the traditional way of reporting on a research study. We have a short summary that is more suited for online reading. In This Article: Introduction Overview of Studies Study 1: Directed Tasks Study 2: Exploratory Study of Reading Study 3: Measurement Study Future Research Conclusions References Introduction "Really good writing - you don't see much of that on the Web," said one of our test participants. And our general impression is that most Web users would agree. Our studies suggest that current Web writing often does not support users in achieving their main goal: to find useful information as quickly as possible. We have been running Web usability studies since 1994 [Nielsen 1994b, Nielsen and Sano 1994, Nielsen 1995]. Our studies have been similar to most other Web usability work (e.g., [Shum 1996, Spool et al. 1997]) and have mainly looked at site architecture, navigation, search, page design, layout, graphic elements and style, and icons. Even so, we have collected many user comments about the content during this long series of studies. Indeed, we have come to realize that content is king in the user's mind: When asked for feedback on a Web page, users will comment on the quality and relevance of the content to a much greater extent than they will comment on navigational issues or the page elements that we consider to be "user interface" (as opposed to simple information). Similarly, when a page comes up, users focus their attention on the center of the window where they read the body text before they bother looking over headerbars or other navigational elements. We have derived three main content-oriented conclusions from our four years' of Web usability studies [Nielsen 1997a]: users do not read on the Web; instead they scan the pages, trying to pick out a few sentences or even parts of sentences to get the information they want users do not like long, scrolling pages: they prefer the text to be short and to the point users detest anything that seems like marketing fluff or overly hyped language ("marketese") and prefer factual information. This latter point is well illustrated by the following quote from a customer survey we ran on the Sun website: "One piece of advice, folks: Let's try not to be so gratuitous and self-inflating. acquisitionResults.content:
SIMULATED proprietary social evidence — no live provider was called.
Observed audience-language patterns for one-person-company founders:
- They describe the pain as "I keep switching between selling, researching, following up, and actually doing the work."
- "AI manager" is often read as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy makes clear that work is actually carried through.
- The strongest desired outcome is one accountable system that can notice missing capability, get what it needs, do the work, and return with a finished result.
- Generic "automate your workflows" language feels broad and tool-like; concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand.
Recommended messaging implication: lead with the founder outcome and accountability, then explain the make-versus-buy capability underneath.

companyArtifacts.content:
Launch page — revised messaging package (version 3; draft for review, not published)

Purpose and launch context
Relaunch today for one-person-company founders. The current signal is low signup conversion and visitors do not recognise themselves. This package is a messaging revision for review; it is not approval to send or publish.
Source: company record launch/context (application observation ev_1790032894378_f6uvrd).

Recommended launch copy

Headline: “Run the business. Somebody keeps the work moving.”

Subhead: “Somebody is an AI manager for one-person companies—helping you turn the work you identify into clear next steps, follow-ups, and progress.”

Supporting copy:
“You’re selling, researching, following up, and doing the work—often at the same time. Somebody helps keep those moving so important work does not disappear between your next task and your next customer.”

“Start with the work that needs attention. Get a clear view of next steps and follow-ups, then stay accountable for what happens next.”

CTA: “See how it keeps my work moving”

Qualification / trust copy
“Somebody is designed for one-person companies and lean teams. It helps organise and move work forward; it does not replace your judgment or guarantee revenue, completed work, or business results. Review its suggestions and decide what to do.”

Audience and problem
Primary audience: one-person-company founders. Do not address the audience as generic “businesses.” Reflect the lived context of switching among selling, researching, following up, and doing the work. Lead with concrete work outcomes—next steps, follow-ups, and visible progress—instead of “automate your workflows,” “too many tools,” or other abstract language.

Positioning decision
Use “AI manager” only with an immediate execution/accountability explanation. The phrase alone may be interpreted as advice, a dashboard, or a generic AI feature. The copy therefore says what the product helps do (turn identified work into next steps, follow-ups, and progress) while avoiding an unsupported claim that it independently completes work. “Helps” and “designed for” are intentional qualifications.

Diagnosis addressed
1. Generic audience and pain: replaced “for your business” with “for one-person companies” and described the founder’s concurrent selling, research, follow-up, and delivery work.
2. Ambiguous “AI manager”: paired the label with specific next-step, follow-up, and progress language and an explicit limitation on replacing judgment.
3. Broad/abstract workflow language: replaced “automate your workflows” with concrete, comprehensible actions and outcomes.

Evidence and limits
The supplied audience-language evidence (acquisition resultEvidenceId: sim_result_8a97ee9287b4bff00ef669a9; provenance: simulated proprietary social evidence) supports using concrete outcome/accountability language and describing the switching-work context. The prior review also identified the three material messaging causes above, with the “AI manager” conclusion treated as a supported diagnosis rather than proof of sole causation. These sources do not establish that this revision will increase conversion, nor do they establish revenue, productivity, or autonomous-completion results. No such claims are made here.

Prior baseline and improvement definition
Prior launch baseline (version 2): headline “Somebody: an AI manager for your business”; subhead “Automate your workflows with AI”; generic-business audience; assumed pain “too many tools”; observed signal: low signup conversion and visitors leaving without signing up. The baseline has no supplied numeric conversion rate, so no numeric lift is claimed.

Improvement means that the revised copy is more specific and testable against that baseline: (a) intended founders can identify themselves in the first screen, (b) a comprehension check identifies the product’s concrete job as helping keep next steps and follow-ups moving, and (c) signup conversion is compared with the unchanged baseline page under the same measurement window and traffic conditions. Record baseline and variant exposure, signup rate, and sample dates before interpreting results. A positive result is not established until measured.

Review and test plan
Before relaunch, review the wording and factual qualifications. Run the revised package against the prior baseline without paid spend. Primary outcome: signup conversion rate. Secondary diagnostic: unaided description of who the product is for and what it does, plus abandonment. Preserve the baseline copy as the control. Report results with exposure counts, dates, and uncertainty; do not infer causation from conversion movement alone if traffic or audience changes.

Open limitations (not critical messaging gaps)
No numeric prior conversion baseline, experiment result, or independent validation of the proposed copy was supplied. No claim of expected lift is made. The package is ready for review and controlled testing, not publication.

history.content:
Launch page — current message
Headline: "Somebody: an AI manager for your business."
Subhead: "Automate your workflows with AI."
Status: launch not converting; visitors leave without signing up.
Assumed audience: generic "businesses".
Assumed pain point: "too many tools".

Launch messaging problem: material causes and uncertainty (for review)

Material cause 1 — audience and pain are too generic.
Evidence: The current page targets generic “businesses” and assumes the pain is “too many tools.” The supplied audience-language evidence instead describes one-person-company founders switching among selling, researching, following up, and doing the work, and says concrete outcome/accountability language is easier to understand than generic workflow language (acquisition resultEvidenceId: sim_result_8a97ee9287b4bff00ef669a9; provenance: simulated proprietary social evidence). Conclusion: the current framing may fail to identify the intended buyer’s lived problem or make the promised outcome salient. This is a supported messaging diagnosis, not proof that audience mismatch is the sole cause of non-conversion.

Material cause 2 — “AI manager” may signal advice or a dashboard rather than completed work.
Evidence: The supplied audience-language evidence reports that “AI manager” is often read as another dashboard or advisor unless the copy makes clear that work is carried through, while the desired outcome is an accountable system that notices missing capability, gets what it needs, does the work, and returns with a finished result (acquisition resultEvidenceId: sim_result_8a97ee9287b4bff00ef669a9; provenance: simulated proprietary social evidence). Conclusion: the headline does not explicitly communicate execution, ownership, or a finished result. Whether visitors in this launch actually interpreted it that way remains unresolved.

Material cause 3 — the subhead is broad and abstract.
Evidence: The current subhead is “Automate your workflows with AI.” The supplied audience-language evidence says generic “automate your workflows” language feels broad and tool-like, while concrete language about owning an outcome and finishing the job is easier to understand (acquisition resultEvidenceId: sim_result_8a97ee9287b4bff00ef669a9; provenance: simulated proprietary social evidence). Public usability evidence from Nielsen Norman Group reports that web users scan rather than read fully and summarizes a study in which concise writing scored 58% higher in measured usability than the control (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/concise-scannable-and-objective-how-to-write-for-the-web/; application observation ev_1790032868239_4o1qtc). Conclusion: the subhead likely does not provide a sufficiently concrete, quickly scannable explanation of who is helped and what gets finished. The public study does not establish this launch’s conversion cause.

Unresolved uncertainty
- No controlled test, visitor interview, funnel breakdown, or direct launch analytics were supplied; therefore the relative contribution of these causes to visitors leaving and not signing up is unknown.
- The supplied audience-language evidence is simulated proprietary evidence and describes observed patterns for one-person-company founders; it does not establish that all visitors are one-person-company founders or that the patterns generalize to the whole launch audience.
- It is unknown whether product capability, trust, pricing, technical friction, traffic quality, or the signup flow also materially affect conversion.
- It is unknown whether “AI manager” performs better or worse than alternative wording for this specific audience.

Review implication (not published): Test a message that names the founder’s concrete job burden, leads with accountable completion of an outcome, and explains the underlying capability afterward. Measure comprehension and signup conversion separately; do not treat the evidence above as proof of causation.

history.changeNote: Version 3: revised launch messaging package for review. Reframed for one-person-company founders, replaced abstract workflow language with concrete next-step/follow-up language, qualified AI-manager and outcome claims, and defined comparison against the supplied qualitative prior baseline without inventing metrics. Preserved prior diagnosis, evidence provenance, uncertainty, and non-publication status.

finalSemanticAssessment.rationale: The artifact meets the relaunch_ready minimum bar. It documents the observed problem and three material messaging causes: generic audience/pain framing, ambiguous “AI manager” positioning, and abstract workflow language. Each is tied to the supplied audience-language evidence and launch context, while uncertainty about causal impact and conversion improvement is explicitly preserved. The revised package directly addresses those causes with audience-specific, concrete copy, appropriate qualifications, a clear baseline comparison, and a controlled test plan that defines primary and secondary outcomes. No critical messaging gap is apparent for review and controlled relaunch preparation, although publication and performance improvement remain unproven.
